1924 Federal-Knight Truck Sat for 70 Years, Sleeve-Valve Engine Wants To Live
10 photos
Photo: Jennings Motor sports/YouTube
Are you a fan of revival videos, but you've seen one too many Chevrolet Tri-Five features? Well, how about seeing a 1924 Federal truck spring back to life? Haven't heard about Federal up until now? No worries, I love to tell stories about orphan brands.
The Federal Motor Truck Company came to be in 1910, but it was actually born as Bailey. It was headquartered in Detroit, Michigan, operating a factory on Leavitt Street. Federal's main competitor was Diamond T, a far more iconic truck manufacturer.
Perhaps the most interesting bit of info about Federal is that it was founded by Martin L. Pulcher, who was part of the small founding group at Oakland Motor Car Company. The latter was purchased by GM and eventually spawned the Pontiac brand in 1926.
Federal was somewhat successful until the late 1940s, with production reaching as many as 3,500 trucks per year. Peak sales hit 10,000 units in 1947. The company was eventually sold to NAPCO, which was famous for four-wheel drive vehicle parts. NAPCO closed down Federal's Detroit plant and moved all tooling to Minneapolis. The company was shut down in March 1960.
The truck you see here was born in 1924, at a time when Federal was doing quite good. 1924 was actually a banner year for the company, as the city of Detroit had officially renamed Leavitt Street to Federal Street. Moreover, it was the second consecutive year when Federal outsold its primary rival, Diamond T.
1924 also marked the introduction of Federal's light delivery truck, powered by a Willys-Knight sleeve-valve engine. It was marketed as the Federal-Knight and remained in production through 1927. This weathered truck is one of those rigs.
Reportedly parked for a whopping 70 years, this hauler is in pretty bad shape overall. But at the same time, it's also in surprisingly good condition for a vehicle that sat for this long. I mean, it's still in one piece, rust isn't terrible yet, and it's still very much complete. Moreover, it still has the original sleeve-valve four-cylinder engine under the hood.
Patented by Charles Knight in 1904, this engine replaced traditional poppet valves, springs, and camshafts with rotating cylindrical sleeves placed around the pistons. Similar engines were also used by Daimler and Panhard, but the design became obsolete after World War II. Knight's engine is a whopping 100 years old, and seeing one in such condition is absolutely amazing.
And you know what's even more amazing? The fact that our host managed to get it to fire up. It doesn't idle just yet, and this truck is far from being road-worthy, but hey, it's definitely better than rotting away in a junkyard.
Will we see this truck back on the road anytime soon? Well, that's a question I cannot answer, and the owner didn't say a word about it. But it's a great opportunity to see a rare Federal truck that's not a rust bucket .
